# Logistics / Supply Chain

**Page type:** detail page (one h2 per pitfall, each followed by a two-column obj-table row: text left 50%, canvas right 50%)
**HTML title tag:** Logistics / Supply Chain - Domain-Specific Data Pitfalls

**Subtitle:** Data pitfalls unique to supply chain analytics, demand forecasting, and inventory optimization

## Callout (philosophy box)

**Core tension:** Supply chain data is generated by a system that reacts to its own predictions. Stock-outs suppress observed demand, promotions distort baselines, and small signals amplify through multi-tier networks. Naive models trained on this data will systematically underestimate demand and misallocate inventory.

## Bullwhip Effect

**Obj-title:** Small demand changes amplify upstream

A 5% change in consumer demand can become an 80% swing at the raw materials level. Each tier in the supply chain over-reacts to perceived changes, adding safety stock and batching orders.

- **Mechanism:** Each node forecasts independently and adds buffer
- **Result:** Variance amplification at every stage
- **Data pitfall:** Upstream data looks volatile but downstream is stable
- **Fix:** Share point-of-sale data across all tiers; do not let each node forecast independently

### Visualization (canvas `canvas1`, 720×260)

Bar chart of order variability rising across supply-chain tiers.

- **Title (bold 15px, `#1a5276`, centered at (360,20)):** "Order Variability Amplification".
- **Y-axis label (rotated 13px `#666` at x=15):** "% Change in Orders".
- **Bars** (width 60, baseline y=220, max height 160 for 80%; evenly spaced from x≈70; bold 15px `#1a5276` value label above each bar; 13px `#333` stage label below):
  - Consumer 5%, Retailer 15%, Distributor 40%, Manufacturer 65%, Supplier 80%
  - Bar color interpolates green→red with variability: rgb channels from (39,174,96) at 0% to (231,76,60) at 80%, fill at 0.8 alpha, 2px solid border in the same interpolated color.
- **Amplification line:** dashed 4/3 `#e74c3c` width-2 line connecting the bar tops, ending in a small red upward arrowhead at the Supplier bar.

## Censored Demand

**Obj-title:** Out of stock = zero sales, not zero demand

When inventory hits zero, sales drop to zero. But demand did not disappear - customers simply left. A model trained on sales data will systematically underestimate true demand for frequently out-of-stock items.

- **Mechanism:** Sales = min(demand, available stock)
- **Result:** Downward bias in demand forecasts
- **Data pitfall:** Zero sales periods treated as zero demand
- **Fix:** Flag stockout periods; use censored regression or impute demand from pre-stockout rates

### Visualization (canvas `canvas2`, 720×260)

Line chart: observed sales collapsing to zero vs hidden true demand over 14 days.

- **Title (bold 15px, `#1a5276`, centered at (360,18)):** "Observed Sales vs True Demand".
- **Axes:** `#ccc` L axes with padding L60/R30/T35/B45; y scale 0–60 with `#eee` gridlines and `#666` labels at 0, 20, 40, 60; x labels "Day 1", "Day 3", … every other day. Rotated y-axis title (12px `#666`): "Units / Day".
- **Data (days 1–14):**
  - True demand (dashed 6/4 `#27ae60`, width 2.5): `[48, 52, 50, 47, 53, 50, 51, 50, 49, 52, 50, 48, 51, 50]`
  - Observed sales (solid `#1a5276`, width 2.5, 3px dots at each point): `[48, 52, 50, 47, 3, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]`
- **Stockout region:** `rgba(231,76,60,0.08)` shaded rectangle from day 5 to day 14, labeled at top (12px `#e74c3c`, centered): "OUT OF STOCK".
- **Legend (13px, below chart):** solid blue line sample "Observed Sales (what model sees)"; dashed green line sample "True Demand (hidden)".

## Promotion Distortion

**Obj-title:** Promotions pull demand forward, not create it

A promotion showing 3x lift looks like success. But the following two weeks show 0.5x sales. Total demand across 3 weeks is roughly the same - customers just bought earlier. The model sees a spike followed by a trough and treats them as separate events.

- **Mechanism:** Pantry loading and deal timing shift purchases in time
- **Result:** Overstated promotion ROI; post-promo "dips" trigger replenishment alerts
- **Data pitfall:** Each week modeled independently loses the pull-forward pattern
- **Fix:** Model demand over the full promotion + recovery window (typically 3-4 weeks)

### Visualization (canvas `canvas3`, 720×260)

Weekly bar chart showing promo spike and post-promo trough against a baseline.

- **Title (bold 15px, `#1a5276`, centered at (360,18)):** "Promotion Pull-Forward Effect".
- **Axes:** `#ccc` L axes with padding L60/R30/T35/B45; y scale 0–350 with `#eee` gridlines and `#666` labels at 0, 100, 200, 300. Rotated y-axis title (12px `#666`): "Units Sold".
- **Bars** (width 55, bold 13px `#1a5276` value above each; 12px week labels below, "PROMO" in bold `#e67e22`):
  - Weeks: Wk 1, Wk 2, Wk 3, PROMO, Wk 5, Wk 6, Wk 7, Wk 8
  - Sales: `[100, 95, 105, 300, 50, 60, 90, 100]`
  - Colors: promo bar fill `rgba(230,126,34,0.7)` stroke `#e67e22`; bars below baseline (50, 60, 90) fill `rgba(231,76,60,0.4)` stroke `#e74c3c`; normal bars fill `rgba(26,82,118,0.35)` stroke `#1a5276`; 1.5px borders.
- **Baseline:** dashed 6/4 `#27ae60` width-2 horizontal line at 100, labeled (12px green, right end): "True baseline = 100".
- **Bracket annotation:** small red bracket under Wk 5–Wk 6 with 11px `#e74c3c` label: "Post-promo dip (demand pulled forward)".

## Substitution Invisible

**Obj-title:** Substitution corrupts demand signals for both products

When Product A is out of stock, customers buy Product B instead. Now A shows zero demand (wrong - it was constrained) and B shows a spike (wrong - it was substitution, not genuine preference). Both signals mislead the model.

- **Mechanism:** Customer switches to available alternative
- **Result:** A gets less future stock (death spiral); B gets overstocked
- **Data pitfall:** Model sees "A demand dropped, B demand surged" - both wrong
- **Fix:** Track stockout co-occurrence; model substitution matrices from assortment experiments

### Visualization (canvas `canvas4`, 720×260)

Two panels of horizontal bars: model's view vs reality, separated by a dashed divider.

- **Title (bold 15px, `#1a5276`, centered at (360,18)):** "Substitution Creates False Demand Signals".
- **Panel headers (bold 13px, centered):** left `#e74c3c` "What Model Sees (Wrong)"; right `#27ae60` "Reality".
- **Bars** (height 30, gap 12; 12px `#333` label left of each bar; bar fill = color + 40% alpha with 1.5px solid border; bold 13px value label "N units" after the bar; zero values shown as a thin 3px `#ddd` marker):
  - Left panel: "Product A Sales" 0 `#e74c3c`; "Product A "Demand"" 0 `#e74c3c`; "Product B Sales" 70 `#e67e22`; "Product B "Demand"" 70 `#e67e22` (max scale 80)
  - Right panel: "Product A Demand" 40 `#27ae60`; "Product A Available" 0 `#999`; "Product B Demand" 30 `#27ae60`; "Product B Substitution" 40 `#2980b9`
- **Divider:** vertical dashed 4/3 `#ccc` line at x=360.
- **Bottom annotations (12px, centered under each panel):** red: "Model concludes: "A demand dropped, B demand surged""; green: "Truth: A demand unchanged; B got A's customers".

## Asymmetric Cost

**Obj-title:** Minimizing forecast error does not minimize cost

Overstock costs $0.50/unit/day (holding). Stockout costs $5/unit/day (lost sale + reputation + expediting). The optimal inventory point is NOT at the demand forecast - it is shifted toward overstocking because the penalty for being under is 10x the penalty for being over.

- **Mechanism:** Holding cost << stockout cost in most supply chains
- **Result:** MSE-optimal forecasts lead to frequent stockouts
- **Data pitfall:** Optimizing accuracy (symmetric loss) when the business problem has asymmetric cost
- **Fix:** Use quantile regression (e.g., 95th percentile) or custom loss weighted by cost ratio

### Visualization (canvas `canvas5`, 720×260)

Asymmetric cost curves around the demand forecast with a shifted optimal point.

- **Title (bold 15px, `#1a5276`, centered at (360,18)):** "Asymmetric Cost: Stockout vs Overstock".
- **Axes:** `#999` horizontal axis with a vertical center line at the demand forecast; padding L60/R40/T35/B50. X labels (12px `#666`): "Understocked" (left), "Inventory Level" and "Demand Forecast" (center, with small gray arrowhead at axis), "Overstocked" (right). X domain -50…+50 units from forecast; y scale 0–120 cost.
- **Curves:**
  - Stockout cost (left half): solid `#e74c3c` width 3, steep quadratic — cost = ((|x|/10)²)×2.5 for x in [-50, 0]
  - Holding cost (right half): solid `#e67e22` width 3, gentle linear — cost = (x/10)×2.2 for x in [0, 50]
  - Total cost: dashed 5/3 `#1a5276` width 2 across the full domain (sum of the two)
- **Optimal point:** green `#27ae60` dot (radius 7, white 2px ring) at x=+12 on the holding curve, labeled bold 13px green "Optimal point" plus 11px lines "(shifted right: better to" / "overstock than stockout)".
- **Naive point:** red `#e74c3c` dot (radius 5) at x=0 on the axis, labeled 11px right-aligned: "MSE-optimal (wrong)".
- **Legend (12px, top left):** red line "Stockout cost ($5/unit/day)"; orange line "Holding cost ($0.50/unit/day)"; dashed blue line "Total cost".

## Regeneration instructions

- **Layout:** standard detail page. h1 + `.subtitle` + one `.philosophy` callout, then one `<h2>` per pitfall followed by an `.obj-table` (full-width, border-collapse) with a single `<tr>`: left `<td>` (45%) holds `.obj-title`, an intro paragraph, and a labeled-bullet `<ul>` (Mechanism / Result / Data pitfall / Fix); right `<td>` (55%, centered) holds the canvas. Even rows background `#fafcfe`.
- **Page CSS:** body system sans-serif (-apple-system stack), white background, text `#2a2a2a`, padding 40px 20px, line-height 1.6; h1 1.8em `#1a5276`; h2 1.4em `#1a5276` with 2px `#2980b9` bottom border; subtitle `#666` 1.05em; paragraphs 0.95em `#333`; bullets 0.9em; cell borders `1px solid #e0e0e0`, padding 20px 24px; `.obj-title` 1.05em weight 600 `#1a5276`; `strong` `#1a5276`; `.philosophy` — background `#f0f4f8`, left border `4px solid #2980b9`, padding 12px 16px, 0.9em. No nav bar, no back/home links.
- **Canvases:** each 720×260 intrinsic; shared `setupCanvas(id, w, h)` helper sizes the backing store to the rendered width × `window.devicePixelRatio` (display capped at the logical width via `style.maxWidth`), and calls `ctx.scale` so drawing stays in logical coordinates. Chart titles bold 15px -apple-system.
- **Palette:** primary blue `#1a5276`, secondary blue `#2980b9`, green `#27ae60`, red `#e74c3c`, orange `#e67e22`, bar fill `rgba(26,82,118,0.35)`, gray text `#333`/`#666`/`#999`.
- In regenerated HTML, any card/page links use `.html` extensions (this page has none).
